title: Where to Approximate in Neurosymbolic Inference?
claim: Many existing approximation methods are specific combinations of exact or approximate choices in one shared three-step pipeline, leaving new combinations open.
layout: 2 parts: left method-by-step table, right circuit diagrams; color-coded operations
description: The left half is a table. Rows are baselines: exact methods, fuzzy methods, Sem Strength, CTSketch, and APRICOT A, B and C. Columns are the three pipeline steps, SI, SII and SIII. Each cell holds a colored operation name such as KC, MUL, INDEP, TT-SVD, PREMUL or ROUNDMUL, or a dash. Orange and yellow mark exact operations. Teal, purple and pink mark approximate ones, as the legend at the bottom shows. The right half has two small diagrams. The first, labeled SDD, shows Boolean clauses compiled by KC into small neural-net-like circuits, which MUL then merges into one circuit. The second, labeled APRICOT, shows input tensors compressed by TT-SVD into tensor-train cores, which MUL and ROUNDMUL merge into one. The eye goes first to the colorful table.
caption: Where can we approximate when compiling structured-decomposable circuits? We unify bottom-up approaches in a three-step pipeline: (Step I) compiles each factor $\phi_j$ into an \hlkc{exact} or \hlfactorb{relaxed} circuit, (Step II) multiplies the resulting $N$ circuits down to $K$ \hlexactb{exactly} or using \hlprodb{recompression strategies}, and (Step III) combines any $K>1$ remaining circuits with an \hlindepb{independence} (fuzzy) approximation. Existing methods correspond to specific combinations of exact or approximate operations, but the framework also allows for new TT-based \apricot strategies yet to be explored.
abstract: Probabilistic neurosymbolic methods rely on weighted model counting (WMC) to combine neural predictors with symbolic constraints. Exact WMC is #P-hard and typically scales poorly, so many methods resort to approximations. By unifying existing approaches under a three-step bottom-up approximate compilation pipeline, we study where approximation budget is best allocated. Inspired by tensor networks, we instantiate two steps with tensor train decompositions and derive new pipelines that exactly multiply approximated factors and recompress their products via SVD- or interpolation-based schemes. Across six tasks in Sudoku, arithmetic reasoning, and scene understanding, and across increasing problem sizes, our pipelines produce WMC estimates orders-of-magnitude more accurate than prior methods. This translates into stronger downstream learning on tasks where reasoning relies on tight interactions between symbolic factors, where cruder approximations ignore these dependencies. Our pipelines open novel design space for effective approximate compilation of challenging probabilistic reasoning tasks.
